reason: The provided sources yield over 12 multi-sourced claims detailing Sagittarius A*'s mass, imaging, flares, and magnetic acceleration.
story: At the heart of the Milky Way, 27,000 light-years away, lies Sagittarius A*, a supermassive black hole four million times the mass of our Sun. Discovered by tracking stars whipping through its extreme gravitational field, this cosmic monster remains largely hidden behind dense interstellar dust. In May 2022, the Event Horizon Telescope combined eight observatories across Earth to capture its image, revealing a glowing ring surrounding a dark shadow. But Sagittarius A* is far from quiet. Extreme magnetic interactions and reconnections in the surrounding hot plasma trigger sudden, violent flares in near-infrared and X-ray light. These magnetic outbursts accelerate subatomic particles and hot spots of gas to 30% of the speed of light, orbiting the event horizon in mere minutes. Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez earned the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics for proving the existence of this terrifying galactic anchor.
angle: At the center of our galaxy, violent magnetic field reconnections near Sagittarius A* whip clumps of gas to 30% of the speed of light in mere minutes.

claims.claim: Sagittarius A* is the supermassive black hole located at the center of the Milky Way galaxy.
Sagittarius A* has a mass approximately four million times that of the Sun.
Sagittarius A* is located roughly 27,000 light-years away from Earth.
Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez were awarded shares of the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics for proving Sagittarius A* is a supermassive compact object.
Astronomers determined the mass of Sagittarius A* by tracking the orbits of stars very close to the galactic center.
In May 2022, astronomers released the first direct image showing the glowing accretion ring and shadow around Sagittarius A*.
The image of Sagittarius A* was produced by the Event Horizon Telescope using eight radio observatories linked across Earth.
Sagittarius A* is the second black hole ever directly imaged, following Messier 87's supermassive black hole in 2019.
Gas orbiting close to Sagittarius A* moves at extreme speeds reaching about 30% of the speed of light.
The brightness and emission pattern of gas around Sagittarius A* change rapidly on a timescale of minutes.
Sagittarius A* produces violent flares observable in near-infrared and X-ray wavelengths.
Magnetic field interactions and magnetic reconnection in the gas surrounding Sagittarius A* accelerate particles and power flares.
Observations using the GRAVITY instrument on the Very Large Telescope detected bright hot spots orbiting close to the black hole.
Sagittarius A* lies in the direction of the constellation Sagittarius as viewed from Earth.
